newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China ship sails into Taiwan with Nationalist flag.
newsitem.headline: China ship sails into Taiwan with Nationalist flag.

text.p: The second ship to sail directly to Taiwan from rival China in 48 years entered the southern Kaohsiung Harbour Sunday, complying with a local requirement to fly Taiwan's Nationalist Republic of China flag.
A harbour control official confirmed the identity of the China-owned Far East Glory and a Reuters reporter at the scene said the ship was flying Taiwan's flag.
Taiwan and China split at the end of a civil war in 1949. Beijing's Chinese communist government regards Nationalist-held Taiwan as a renegade province.
A dispute over the flag had postponed the arrival of the ship, which had moored outside Kaohsiung port for five hours before entering at sunset.

Although Saturday's long-awaited first crossing from China to Taiwan went smoothly, problems emerged on Sunday as the second ship grappled with a maritime custom which calls for ships to fly the flag of their host port.
On Saturday, the Sheng Da made a historic voyage to Taiwan after the rival sides of the Taiwan Strait eased restrictions on shipping.
The Sheng Da removed Taiwan's Republic of China flag after briefly flying it as it entered Kaohsiung port.
Taiwan port officials later said that in line with international practice, foreign-registered ships were allowed to remove the flag of the host port after sunset.
"There is no point flying the flag at night," Yu Fang-lai, director of Kaohsiung Harbour Bureau, told reporters.
"What was most important was the breakthrough in more than four decades of the shipping (link) between the sides of the Taiwan Strait," he said.
Taiwan, which has banned direct links with China since 1949, has agreed to allow limited direct shipping with the mainland in the hope of improving ties with Beijing.
Under this scheme, mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs but can be processed at Kaohsiung's new "offshore trans-shipment centre" for onward passage to third countries.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be loaded on ships planning to cross directly to the Chinese mainland.
Taiwan's shipping company officials said both Sheng Da and Far East Glory were reluctant to fly the flag because of the sensitive politics behind it.
That was why they waited until sunset to enter port, they added.
"Flying the flag is tantamount to recognising the sovereignty of Taiwan," one official said.
But the ship's Taiwan agent denied the delay was intentional.
"It was mainly because our pier was occupied by a huge Korean container ship," said Jacy Shin, ship planner chief of the Taiwan agent, Ocean Pioneer Shipping Co.
